title: Decision: the live stream is kept alive by WebSocket Pings both ends send
description:
Mark, 2026-11-27: "transport ping for the live stream, send it ourselves", choosing option 3 of bead mimid-j729 over an application-level probe in the binding.

BEFORE. Version 1 of the live stream had no keepalive in either direction. ClientMessage was Hello or Request, ProviderMessage was Hello, Ack, Error, Deliver, Position or Changed, nothing in mimid ever sent a WebSocket Ping, and a Ping or Pong that arrived was dropped unread by both ends, tungstenite having answered it inside the library. An idle carrier a middlebox had reaped looked exactly like a healthy idle carrier until the next request timed out.

CHOSEN. Both ends send WebSocket Pings themselves (RFC 6455 5.5.2), with one constant, mimid_live::PING_AFTER, 30 seconds. Either end probes after PING_AFTER of quiet and ends the connection if nothing at all has arrived by the next probe, so a dead carrier is noticed within twice that. Any frame counts as a sign of life, a Pong included: the far end's library answers a Ping only while that end is reading, so a Pong proves its read loop is turning. Nothing is added to the binding's own messages, so there is no version bump and no CDDL change.

WHAT IT ASSERTS, and this is the whole point of choosing the transport: that the pipe is there and the far end is reading. NOT that the provider can serve a request, which is what an application-level probe would have asserted and what bead mimid-f9x4 would have MIMI define. A provider wedged behind its database still answers Pings, as the IRC front end used to before decision mimid-1wgh.132.

30 SECONDS, chosen under the 60 seconds where deployed NATs and load balancers reap an idle TCP connection, whatever RFC 5382 5 asked for. INVENTED VALUE, NOT FROM SPEC: MIMI has no keepalive to take one from.

THE PROVIDER'S SIDE takes the interval from JmapOptions::live_ping_after, so a test probes in milliseconds. A Ping is queued with try_send and never waits for room: a full queue means the client is not reading what it already has, so a probe would say nothing and waiting would park the connection's loop. The hello now has one deadline for the whole exchange rather than one per read, since a client that sent nothing but Pings could otherwise hold a pre-authentication connection open for as long as it liked.

THE AGENT'S SIDE has no knob: its writer task probes at the constant, and the reader counts every frame so the writer can tell whether anything came back. A connection the writer gives up on is marked not alive, which is the path the stream already had for a lost connection, so the sync loop reconnects.

THE CLOSE IS SILENT. Neither end sends an Error first: there is no code for "you stopped answering", and the peer that has stopped answering would not read it.
